content: Human parainfluenza virus (HPIV) is an enveloped virus with a single-stranded, negative-sense RNA genome. It is classified into four distinct serotypes: HPIV-1, HPIV-2, HPIV-3, and HPIV-4. The viral genome is approximately 15,000 nucleotides in length and encodes six structural proteins. These proteins are essential for the virus to attach to, enter, and fuse with host cells, forming a complex with the RNA genome. HPIV belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family and is further categorized into two genera based on its serotype: Respirovirus (which includes HPIV-1 and HPIV-3) and Rubulavirus (which includes HPIV-2 and HPIV-4). The virus is primarily transmitted through respiratory droplets expelled during coughing or sneezing. It can also spread via direct physical contact with an infected individual or by touching surfaces contaminated with the virus. HPIV infects the body by targeting specific types of white blood cells, including histiocytes, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils. The virus uses two glycoproteins, hemagglutinin-neuraminidase and fusion protein, to bind to and fuse with the host cell membrane. Once fusion occurs, the viral nucleocapsid is released into the cytoplasm of the host cell. Viral transcription is carried out by a virus-specific RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which synthesizes viral mRNAs. These mRNAs are subsequently translated into viral proteins. The replication of the viral genome involves the synthesis of both positive-sense and negative-sense RNA strands. The negative-sense RNA strand is encapsidated by nucleoprotein and serves as a template for further transcription and replication, ensuring the production of new viral particles.
